title: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co. (2010)
summary: The action could seek federal class treatment despite New York’s statutory restriction, but the Justices divided over the Rules Enabling Act analysis.
notes:
This did not certify the proposed class or erase Rule 23’s prerequisites. It also does not make every state rule affecting a class action invalid in federal court. Record the distinct scope and validity questions and the fractured reasoning.

Shady Grove treated Sonia Galvez after a car accident and took an assignment of her Allstate benefits; Allstate paid late and refused the 2% statutory interest, worth about $500 to Shady Grove but roughly $5 million class-wide; N.Y. C.P.L.R. 901(b) bars class actions to recover statutory penalties, and the Eastern District of New York dismissed for lack of CAFA jurisdiction, with the Second Circuit affirming.

Justice Scalia's plurality asked only whether Rule 23 'really regulates procedure' (Sibbach), while Justice Stevens's controlling concurrence would hold a Federal Rule inapplicable where it would displace a state rule so intertwined with a state right or remedy that it functions to define the scope of the state-created right; Justice Ginsburg's dissent, joined by Justices Kennedy, Breyer and Alito, read Rule 23 and § 901(b) as not in conflict.

sections.Parties: Shady Grove, holding assigned claims for unpaid statutory interest, sued Allstate and sought to represent a class.
sections.Material Facts: The individual interest claim was modest, while the proposed class allegations placed a much larger amount at stake. New York’s provision restricted class actions seeking statutory penalties. Federal Rule 23 prescribed the conditions for a federal class action. The issue was whether the state restriction added a further barrier even if the federal Rule’s conditions were met.
sections.Procedural History: The lower federal courts applied the state restriction. The Supreme Court reversed, with five Justices supporting the conclusion that Rule 23 governed the relevant question but divided reasoning about its validity as applied.
sections.Issue: Did Rule 23 displace New York’s restriction on this type of class action, and could it validly do so under the Rules Enabling Act?
sections.Holding: Yes in this case. The state restriction did not prevent seeking class treatment under the applicable Federal Rule.
sections.Reasoning: The majority on scope concluded that the two provisions addressed the same question: whether the action could proceed as a class. Justice Scalia’s plurality then focused on whether Rule 23 regulated the manner and means of enforcing rights. Justice Stevens agreed with the result but maintained that applying a Federal Rule could violate the Enabling Act when it displaced a state provision intertwined with a substantive right or remedy. He did not find that problem with the general New York restriction here. The dissent instead read the state restriction as limiting a remedy in a way that could coexist with Rule 23. Those differences matter when applying the case to a new state provision.

learning.why: The action could seek federal class treatment despite New York’s statutory restriction, but the Justices divided over the Rules Enabling Act analysis.

topics.cp-rule-scope: The majority found Rule 23 answered the class-treatment question addressed by New York’s restriction.
topics.cp-rules-enabling: The Justices divided over how to evaluate effects on state substantive rights.
topics.cp-class-actions: The holding removed the particular state barrier; it did not establish that all Rule 23 certification requirements were satisfied.
topics.cp-precedent: Justice Stevens supplied the decisive concurrence while disagreeing with the plurality’s broad Enabling Act approach.
topics.cp-usc-2072: The Justices split over how § 2072(b)'s 'abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right' limit applies to Rule 23.
topics.cp-frcp-23: The case holds Rule 23 to be a categorical statement of when a class may be certified in federal court.
topics.cp-cafa: Federal jurisdiction depended on CAFA's $5 million threshold, which the class allegations met only if a class could be certified.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Stevens’s concurrence supplied the fifth vote for the outcome while rejecting a wholly facial, procedure-only account of the Enabling Act. Justice Ginsburg’s dissent, joined by three Justices, emphasized state substantive policy and a reading that avoided direct conflict.
